title: 'I'm sorry, but I want you to shoot me!'
article: Most armed robbers plan to get away with their crimes. Not Arthur George Provencal.

Provencal, 34, walked up to the prescription counter at a downtown Calgary pharmacy, pulled a large butcher knife and announced that he wanted to die. What happened next had all the markings of a phenomenon called suicide by cop.

"Kill me, put me out of my misery," Provencal told the pharmacist after taking several hostages and demanding a lethal dose of injectable drugs. When the pharmacist refused, Provencal grabbed him from behind and pressed the blade of the butcher knife to his throat.

It was just before 6 p.m. on Dec. 23. Calgary's TD Square was bustling with last-minute Christmas shoppers as carols played over the mall's sound system. Moments later, a Calgary police officer inside the drugstore repeatedly ordered Provencal to drop the knife. When Provencal ignored the warnings, the officer fired a single shot from his 9-mm Glock handgun. The bullet struck Provencal in the head near the right eye. He was taken to hospital and pronounced dead.
But the "victim" in Provencal's death, says one expert who has studied this form of homicide, is the police officer who was compelled to pull the trigger.
"He's going to have to live with that for the rest of his life," said criminologist Rick Parent, a veteran police constable with the Delta Police Department in suburban Vancouver.
"When people start talking about Christmas, he's going to be thinking about this violent scene and how he shot and killed this guy."

In a landmark study, Parent examined fatal police shootings in British Columbia from 1980 to 1994. He sifted through each case thoroughly in interviews with the police officers involved in the shootings as well as the friends and families of those who were killed.
His surprising conclusion was that in 10 per cent of the shootings, people had wanted police to kill them.

"In some of these cases, police were confronted in a calculated and deliberate manner by people who were suffering from one, or a combination of, suicidal tendencies, mental illness and substance abuse," Parent stated in the thesis for his master's degree on the subject of "victim-precipitated homicide."
"In many cases, suicidal individuals have engaged in life threatening behaviour in order to force the police to kill them."

Such incidents are emotionally traumatic for the police officers involved, Parent learned, causing psychological effects including depression, guilt, nightmares, flashbacks and a heightened sense of danger and fear.
"Your mind can't cope with this," one officer told him. "Sleep? I'd wake up every night for several months. I would never relive the incident but my mind would focus on the incident."

Another officer likened the flashbacks to "a video going on in your head that you can't control; it just keeps playing the video over and over and over again and you've got no control to turn it off."

Physical effects for some included loss of appetite and a marked decrease in sex drive. "My sex life went down the tube, forget about that," said one officer. Several officers who were involved in a fatal shooting said their family life crumbled after the incident.

For some, the shooting became a family crisis. "My wife needed (psychological) help after the incident," said one officer. Another officer's wife developed an eating disorder. "We both know it was in response to me killing the guy," the officer related. "Even though it has been years since the shooting, she still suffers with the disorder and a few other things."
Another officer told Parent how he thought he was coping with the stress until his emotional well-being shattered six months after the fatal shooting incident.

"I thought everything was OK. It (the shooting) didn't bother me. I was tough. Then suddenly when I was out shopping with my wife and kids I had to park the car in the shopping centre. I had this urge to cry. I couldn't control it. Once I started I couldn't stop. My wife had to drive us home. It (the weeping) lasted for days."
Several officers told Parent that the coroner's inquest was a pivotal point in coming to terms with the shooting.

"When it's finished, it's probably the biggest relief the officer experiences because it has been dealt with in a public forum. The facts are laid out and everybody knows what they are. In most cases the officer has nothing to hide. They're quite open about what happened but they can't say it until it comes to court because of the way the system works."

Parent has also studied the "why" of suicide by cop. "It's difficult to take your own life," he said in an interview. "The best example is putting your hand in a fire. You may want to burn yourself, but you've got that physiological factor that forces you to pull your hand away. It's the same if you go to jump from a building or put a gun to your head. It's a lot harder to do, I think, than people imagine."
As well, he said, some people provoke police to shoot them to avoid the social or religious stigma of suicide.
"They may do it if they believe that if they die by someone else's hand they'll go to heaven, whereas if they kill themselves they'll go to hell."
But most cases fall into two main categories, he explained.

"One is the hardened criminal who has done a lot of time and doesn't want to go back to jail. He feels that this is it, `I've had a bad life and if I die I'm gonna go out in a blaze of glory. It's gonna be a Bonnie-and-Clyde type ending.'
"The other category is more the business or factory worker who has had a quiet life and wants some meaning to the way they die. This is their final statement, their swan song in getting out of life."

Parent's interest in the suicide-by-cop phenomenon was sparked by his involvement in a hostage-taking incident in 1990. It began when a man who had fled Vancouver with his three-year-old son a day earlier was spotted in a pick-up truck on Highway 17 in Delta.

"I wound up being involved in a high-speed chase with the guy. We shot out the tires and got the car stopped and it was like a Mexican standoff. It was daytime and the sirens were blaring. He had a shotgun on his lap and he wouldn't come out of the car."
It was then Parent made what he calls "a calculated risk."

"I ran up to the car, smashed the window, and I reached in and grabbed the guy. And as I was smashing the window, I knew he could fire the shotgun and I'd be dead. At the same time, I had my handgun out and it was maybe an inch away from his face and I was prepared to shoot and kill him."
Parent was troubled when he looked back on the incident, even though it ended with only minor injuries from flying glass. The little boy was unharmed.

"I guess I did everything properly because I pulled him out the window and we got the shotgun away from him. But in hindsight, I wasn't happy about it. Emotionally, it sort of bothered me. It wasn't like the Clint Eastwood movies I'd grown up with in the 1970s."
As the incident was happening, Parent experienced what's known as "critical incident stress."

"Everything slowed down and went into slow motion. The sirens that were blaring maybe two metres from my head all of a sudden went quiet. I could hear the glass breaking and certain things were burned into my mind, like his face. It's like a video that's in your head. Even though the incident was positive operationally, it wasn't positive emotionally for me.

"So that's why I got into it. I was going to university, and I thought, `Geez, nobody has ever studied this.' I had heard of people baiting the police but I hadn't realized it was a significant factor. When you start adding mental illness, substance abuse and the bravado, it's quite high. Up to a third of all police shootings fall into that broad category."

Shortly after Parent completed his thesis, the case of Moshe Pergament attracted wide media attention. Pergament, a 19-year-old New York college student with heavy gambling debts, planned his death with particular attention to detail.

On Nov. 14, 1997, Pergament began driving erratically along the Long Island Expressway in his brand-new Honda Accord. When a police cruiser flashed its lights, Pergament pulled over. He jumped out of the car with a plastic replica .38 calibre gun in his hand. The police officer in the cruiser ordered him to drop the gun, but Pergament didn't. He kept on coming, and the officer fired when he was about two metres away.

After the ambulance had taken his body away, detectives found an envelope on the front seat of the Honda. It was addressed "To the Officer who shot me." Inside was a Hallmark card with a tragic note: "Officer, it was a plan. I'm sorry to get you involved. I just needed to die. Please remember that this was all my doing. You had no way of knowing. Moe Pergament."
In Canada, about 10 people die each year at the hands of the police, compared with about 400 per year in the U.S., Parent said.

A U.S. study that followed Parent's research methods found that slightly more than one in 10 fatal shootings by officers of the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department were suicide attempts. University of Southern California researchers looked at 437 officer- involved shootings from 1987-97. They found that suicide by cop accounted for 46 cases or 11 per cent of the total.

The study created a profile of those who decide to end their lives this way -- 98 per cent were men and 39 per cent of those had a history of domestic violence. Major characteristics included a past history of suicide attempts and a high incidence of alcohol and drug dependency.
The split second it takes for a cop to squeeze a trigger is "perhaps the mostly widely seen and least understood event of our time," Parent concluded in a research paper.

"I think police get on the job thinking, `It's not going to happen to me,' " Parent said in an interview. "And secondly, `If it does happen to me, it's going to be clean and obvious and it's going to be a bad person like Clifford Olsen. If I have to do it, it's going to be like I'm saving the day.' What you find is that it's not like that.

"It happens when you least expect it. It's extremely complicated, and maybe it's not a bad guy but somebody crying out for help. And due to circumstances you wind up killing him and it's messy, emotionally traumatic. It's like a roller-coaster ride. Most police don't expect that."

In the past five years many Canadian police forces have formed "critical incident debriefing teams" to help officers involved in shootings, Parent said. "These critical debriefers are peers who are trusted within the organization," he explained.
"The officer can tell them something in confidence, like `I'm shit scared' or `I'm terrified with what's happening' and they can start crying.' "
The debriefing occurs before the province's special investigations unit or detectives from the force's homicide investigation unit interview the officer.
"In the 1980s, there was very little training and there wasn't as much accountability as there is now. Police being recruited now come in at a fairly high level, the training level is high."

With growing awareness of the phenomenon, police are developing new strategies to better handle suicidal people they encounter, said Parent, including the use of Tasers, bean bag guns and other non- lethal weapons.
"Part of it is the research that's going on and part of it is the technology. They've developed a Taser now that's virtually 100-per- cent guaranteed to bring the person down without hurting them."

Police officers in Vancouver and its suburbs now carry Tasers, he said. "Not just the emergency response team, but average officers too. So when they go to a call -- it may be a disturbance or a domestic -- they've got a Taser with them in their pocket. And if opportunity arises to use a less lethal weapon and they can, they have it right there to hand. So that's a good thing. Things are changing in the right direction."
But Parent, who has been a cop since 1980, notes that the police are virtually the only agency in western society that's available 24 hours of every day.
"Police are working all the time -- I worked New Year's Eve and Christmas -- and they go to basically anything and try to solve the problem whatever it is, social or criminal.

"It doesn't happen very often but sometimes police will come across something like a robbery or a murder in progress. And as they come into it they literally have 20 seconds to de-escalate the situation. And if the person wants to confront them, the officer doesn't have any choice but to kill them or to die himself.
"That's the only two choices."
